Henry John Temple, 3rd Viscount Palmerston. The embodiment of mid-Victorian assertiveness as Foreign Secretary and Prime Minister, pursuing aggressive gunboat diplomacy to expand British interests and reshape international law.

Palmerston dominated British foreign policy for three decades, intervening in Portugal, Greece, and the Ottoman Empire to extend British influence and weaken rivals. He became a national hero after the Opium War from 1840 to 1842, which he championed as Foreign Secretary to open Chinese markets to British trade. Though internationally condemned as imperialism, the victory cemented his reputation as a decisive statesman willing to use force to achieve British aims.

His phrase "might is right" captured the philosophy that British naval supremacy and willingness to use force were the supreme tools of diplomacy. He led Britain through the Crimean War from 1853 to 1856, fighting Russia to prop up the Ottoman Empire and prevent Russian expansion toward India. Palmerston backed independence movements against autocratic powers in Italy and the Balkans, positioning Britain as the defender of Protestant nationalism and liberal institutions.

His tenure at the Foreign Office spanned 1830 to 1841 and then 1846 to 1851, while his time as Prime Minister ran from 1855 to 1858 and then 1859 to 1865. He died in office in 1865, still serving as PM at the age of eighty, and was mourned as the last embodiment of British dominance unchallenged by rival powers.
